- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).

## Portals & design system

**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.

- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).

- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).

- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.

- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).

## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session

`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.

1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.

If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).

## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)

- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). Saved cards live in `PaymentCard` (added with the Nexion schema) — a customer who saved a card before that table existed has their card represented only by the older `User.stripeCustomerId`/`stripePaymentMethodId` columns; `hasChargeableCard`/renewals read those directly and are unaffected, but the Billing page's card list reads `PaymentCard`, so a pre-existing card needs the one-off backfill (`scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts`) to show up there. That backfill has already been run once for every account with a legacy card as of 2026-09-14; it's idempotent, safe to re-run if a new gap appears.
- **Namecheap** (`lib/namecheap.ts`): `NAMECHEAP_API_USER/KEY/USERNAME/CLIENT_IP` (+`NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX=1` for testing) → domain search/register/renew/DNS management. TLD retail prices in `TLD_PRICES`.
- **GitHub**: remote `origin` = `git@github.com:santino1233/nxeon.git` via deploy key `/root/.ssh/nxeon_deploy`. Every commit auto-pushes via `.git/hooks/post-commit`. `.env`/credentials are gitignored — never commit secrets.

## Conventions

- All state changes to VMs go through `Job` rows — the web app never calls Proxmox mutation endpoints directly (read-only status calls are OK).
- One in-flight job per server (enforced in `serverAction`).
- Admin-only actions live in [lib/actions.ts](lib/actions.ts) and must call `requireAdmin()`.
- Free VPSes: `Server.isFree = true`, no billing, `expiresAt = null`.
- Wallet amounts are integer cents.
- Never fabricate: no invented stats, ratings, reviews, player counts, or ETAs. If a number can't be read from the database or a real upstream, the field stays empty and the UI says why — this tree has had hash-derived star ratings and fake reviews removed once already.
- Minecraft subdomains (`*.play.nxeon.cloud`) are shared across two tables — `FreeMinecraftServer.subdomain` and `Server.subdomain` — because both products resolve under the same DNS zone. Always check availability through `lib/game-subdomain.ts`'s `isSubdomainAvailable()` (queries both) rather than checking either table alone, or a free and a paid server can claim the same name.

## Documentation — keep it current (required)

- **Every change, fix, or addition MUST update `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` in the same commit.** Add a dated bullet to §15 (Change history) and edit any section the change affects (data model, subsystems, feature catalog, integrations, roadmap, etc.). A commit that changes behaviour without touching the docs is incomplete.
- Keep `ROADMAP.md` in sync too: check off / move the item you completed.
- `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` is the single source of truth. The public mirror at `https://revsports.ca/docs` is regenerated from it with `node scripts/publish-docs.mjs` (zero-dep markdown→styled-HTML renderer → `/var/www/nxeon-docs/index.html`) — run that after editing the doc so the hosted page matches. The `/docs` nginx location lives in `scripts/configure-domains.sh` so it survives vhost regeneration.
- The claude.ai artifact webpage (`https://claude.ai/code/artifact/9b0c97f5-4c34-4f89-bee9-b5a80eb23892`) can only be updated from an interactive Claude Code session (headless/cron runs can't reach it) — that refresh is best-effort, the repo doc + `/docs` page are authoritative.

## Commands

- Typecheck: `npx tsc --noEmit` (always, before a build)
- Build: `npm run build` (must pass before restarting services)
- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
- Worker logs: `journalctl -u nxeon-worker -f`
- E2E test: `npx tsx scripts/e2e-test.ts` (orders a real VM; delete it afterwards via a DELETE job)
- Admin credentials: `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`

## Domains & TLS

- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
- Secure cookies are on (`COOKIE_SECURE=1`) now that real HTTPS exists. Stripe webhook is live at `https://BASE_DOMAIN/api/stripe/webhook`.

## Environments

- **Production**: `/opt/nxeon`, DB `nxeon`, services `nxeon-web` (port 3000) + `nxeon-worker`, nginx port 80, VPS pools IP 10.20.0.100–250 / SSH ports 20000–29999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD`. Public: http://51.79.162.96
- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
- Instance differences are driven entirely by `.env` (NXEON_ENV, NXEON_COOKIE_NAME, NXEON_NAT_CHAIN, NXEON_TAG, NXEON_IP_START/END, NXEON_SSH_PORT_START/END, NXEON_CRED_FILE, PORT, APP_URL) — the code is identical.
- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.

## Safety rules

- NEVER touch VMIDs 9000–9999 (templates) except to add new templates.
- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.
- Never `qm destroy` a VM that has a `Server` row — always go through a DELETE job.
- Never `pkill -f` by pattern on this box — kill by port PID or systemd unit instead (a pattern match has restarted live production before).
- Do not commit `.env`. Do not print the Proxmox token into logs or docs.
- Always `git commit` working states; never leave the tree broken — services restart from this directory.

content.thinking: I need to look through the full refundPayment function in actions-admin-billing.ts to understand its implementation.

I'm noting that refundPayment is the admin path for per-invoice refunds, and that when an invoice gets refunded, its commission needs to be reversed proportionally—since commission is based on net pre-tax base while refundedCents is gross including tax, I need to calculate the proportional reversal amount correctly.

The tricky part is handling multiple partial refunds on the same invoice, since the unique constraint only allows one REFUND row per invoice. I'm thinking through options: either update the existing REFUND row's amount if it's still unsettled, or compute the reversal target cumulatively based on total refunded-to-date divided by invoice total, capped at 1.0.

For the original ACCRUED row specifically, a full refund should VOID it cleanly, but a partial refund can't fully void it — so I need a negative ACCRUED REFUND row that nets correctly at settlement time, which actually works uniformly for both PAID and ACCRUED originals in the outstanding-balance calculation.

The tricky case is multiple partial refunds: the unique constraint on invoiceId+kind means only one REFUND row can exist, so if it's still ACCRUED I can update it with a compare-and-swap, but once it's been settled in a payout I can't touch it anymore — meaning a second partial refund after settlement needs a different discriminator or a redesigned uniqueness key altogether.

I'm leaning toward the cumulative approach: track invoice.refundedCents directly and derive the reversal from the difference against what's already been reversed, since that's idempotent and self-correcting rather than relying on discrete refund event rows.

I realize VOIDing gets messy if an ACCRUED REFUND row already exists, so I'll simplify: only VOID on the very first full reversal, otherwise increment an existing ACCRUED REFUND row using CAS on its amount, or create a new one if the existing row is already PAID. I'm also weighing whether the unique constraint on [invoiceId, kind] still matters once idempotency is handled by comparing against cumulative state, especially under concurrent calls computing overlapping deltas.

Also, Postgres treats NULLs as distinct in unique constraints, which would break original-row idempotency unless I default the reversal column to 0 for originals. But then uniqueness relies on kind being deterministically inferred from a stable invoice description, which feels like a weaker guarantee than I'd like.

I'm weighing whether accrueCommissionForInvoice's existing "no commission" filter plus an explicit check is enough, versus introducing a dedicated discriminator column instead of overloading kind, since kind having three original values means [invoiceId, kind] could still allow multiple original rows per invoice.

A cleaner option: add REFUND as a kind value plus a `refundSeq` column defaulting to 0, with uniqueness on [invoiceId, refundSeq]. The original row always keeps refundSeq 0 (preserving the original per-invoice uniqueness guarantee), while each refund gets the next sequential number, and concurrent refund attempts computing the same seq would collide on the unique constraint and one would lose, forcing a retry or no-op.

I'm weighing whether a simpler single cumulative REFUND row would suffice instead, but that breaks down if the refund row is already settled when another partial refund arrives — though given the rarity of refunds and the short window, that edge case may be acceptable.

For the ACCRUED case, the brief explicitly says to VOID a fully-refunded original while preserving the audit trail; for partial refunds against an ACCRUED commission, a negative REFUND row nets cleanly at settlement rather than mutating the original.

I'm working through a sequential-refund edge case: after a first partial reversal leaves a remainder, adding another negative row for that remainder keeps the math correct without extra mutation, so I'll only VOID when the first reversal is a full one against an ACCRUED original — otherwise I'll add rows. This also ties into the owner's payout rule: whether a commission has already been paid out determines if the reversal reduces what's owed now or hits next month's balance, and either the VOID or negative-row approach should satisfy that.

I'm realizing the outstanding calculation (lifetime minus paid, floored at zero) hides negative balances — if a refund exceeds new earnings, the debt is mathematically carried forward in the totals but invisible in the outstanding display, so I probably need a separate signed balance field to surface that to admins and partners.

The settlement function already guards correctly: it clamps outstanding at zero and refuses to settle when there's nothing owed, so no negative payouts can slip through, though I'm double-checking how negative refund rows interact with the outstanding calc when the balance is still net positive.

That partner funnel logic counting customers with any commission row (including VOID) is a pre-existing detail, not something to fix here. For first-commission conversion tracking, a REFUND row alone shouldn't really count as a conversion if the original was fully voided, though a PAID original with a later REFUND still counts — a minor inconsistency but probably acceptable to leave as is.

I'm now realizing REFUND rows never exist without a non-VOID original, since a full first-time refund goes to VOID status instead. So REFUND rows always accompany a non-VOID original, meaning min(createdAt) isn't affected either way. The bigger issue is that the analytics charges count, which groups by status excluding VOID, would incorrectly count REFUND rows as separate charges — I'm weighing whether to exclude REFUND kind from that groupBy, but that would also strip refunds out of the accrued/paid sums, which isn't quite right either.

I think I'll leave the commission series and totals including negative refund amounts as-is for net earned, and treat the "charges" count display as a minor cosmetic inaccuracy to possibly patch later rather than digging deeper now. Also noting that the dashboard's per-customer charges count via `_count._all` has the same REFUND-inclusion issue — a small display quirk showing 3 charges instead of 2 charges plus 1 refund, worth a light fix eventually but not urgent.

Now I'm turning to the `invoice.partnerCommission` one-to-one relation becoming a list `partnerCommissions PartnerCommission[]`, which means any query checking `partnerCommission: null` will need to be rewritten against the new array-based relation.

I'm now walking through all the refund code paths to understand where reversal logic needs to hook in — starting with the admin refund flow that handles both invoice-linked refunds (which can trigger commission reversal) and standalone refunds unlinked to any invoice, which can't be mapped back to a commission at all.

Then I'm considering the self-serve cancellation flow that issues a prorated refund as wallet credit rather than cash, and questioning whether that counts as a "refund" for the owner's rule that refunds should reduce commission earned, given the money never actually leaves the platform.

content.thinking:
I'm noting that card payments flow into a wallet as top-ups rather than mapping directly to invoices, so a chargeback pulls back wallet funds without a clear link to which specific invoice or commission it should affect — it's ambiguous, likely tied to whatever order was placed around the same time as the top-up.

Since there's no existing chargeback handling at all, I'm weighing whether to add an admin action like "Record chargeback" on a specific invoice that reverses the partner's commission, though it's unclear whether it should also touch invoice status or refund fields without an actual Stripe refund or wallet debit. Given the owner's intent that chargebacks and refunds should claw back earned commission, I'm leaning toward the minimal implementation: an admin-triggered commission reversal tied to a chosen invoice, rather than trying to build a fully automated chargeback detection system.

A cleaner variant might be putting a "Reverse commission (chargeback)" action directly on each commission row in the partner ledger page, letting the admin specify the charged-back amount (defaulting to full) and reusing the same shared reversal function with a "chargeback" reason — since disputes already require human review via Stripe's own notifications, a manual admin trigger feels appropriate rather than building automatic webhook-based dispute handling, which would need payment-intent-to-invoice mapping and dashboard event configuration and is better left as a follow-up. I'm also weighing whether this fits with treating invoice.refundedCents as the source of truth for cumulative reversals.

For idempotency I think the reversal function should take a cumulative refundedCents value rather than the amount of a single refund step — retries with the same cumulative value become no-ops, and distinct partial refunds naturally produce distinct values. That works cleanly for admin-issued refunds where the invoice's post-CAS refundedCents is already the exact cumulative figure, and for domain-transfer or failed-registration refunds where the full amount applies, but I'm still working out how the prorated termination refund — computed from the server's refundable term cash rather than tied directly to an invoice — should map into this same mechanism.

I need to be careful since refundedCents affects lifetime revenue calculations elsewhere, so I want to avoid touching domain-transfer's invoice semantics beyond what's strictly necessary — the minimal fix is to reverse with explicit amounts, letting the sweep backstop only handle the refundPayment case with refundedCents>0 and REFUNDED status.

Weighing whether the sweep backstop is worth the added complexity: the post-commit best-effort call could fail due to a DB error or process crash, both rare, but since accrual already has a sweep for uniform coverage across charge paths, a similar backstop for invoice-detectable refunds seems cheap to add in reconcilePartnerCommissions. I'm working through the idempotency here — the sweep computes cumulative from invoice status, and for refunds not reflected on the invoice (like cancelService or worker refunds), cumulative stays at zero so the delta is negative and it's a safe no-op, meaning the sweep never un-reverses. Still, there's a subtlety in how the cumulative model mixes sources when a worker reconcile fully refunds an invoice versus what the sweep independently computes.

I'm now spotting a real flaw: if cancelService reverses 50% and then a separate card refund covers another 30%, the cumulative model based on invoice refundedCents would see 30% and treat it as already satisfied by the earlier 50% reversal, under-reversing the commission relative to the 80% actually refunded to the customer. This points toward needing event-keyed idempotency instead of a single cumulative source of truth — giving each refund event (invoice step, cancelService, worker job, transfer) its own unique key stored on the REFUND row via a nullable refundKey column with a composite unique constraint, relying on Postgres treating NULLs as distinct so existing rows aren't affected.

For the full-refund case where an ACCRUED row has no prior reversals, I'm using a conditional update to VOID it instead of inserting a negative reversal row, and computing per-event reversal amounts capped by what remains so repeated or partial refunds stay idempotent and can't exceed the original invoice total.

If a partial payout was already made, the refund correctly reduces lifetime earnings while leaving the paid amount intact, so the negative balance carries forward into the next cycle as the owner rule intends. I'm working out where each REFUND row's fields come from — partner/customer/invoice from the original, negative baseCents scaled by the refund fraction, same rate, and a reversalKey tied to the event — so partial refunds on ACCRUED rows net out correctly at settlement.

I also need to check timing edge cases: refunds that happen before accrual, where the reversal would find nothing to reverse and the later accrual sweep either skips (full refund flips invoice to REFUNDED) or wrongly accrues full commission on a partially-refunded invoice, since the sweep only checks invoice status and doesn't account for partial or wallet-credit refunds.

I need to check whether accrueRecentCommissionsForCustomer actually gets called for disk-expand jobs — if not, a failure-then-refund could beat the sweep and cause it to accrue on an already-refunded invoice. A cleaner fix might be to have the reversal function itself call accrueCommissionForInvoice first (idempotent, so it's a no-op if already accrued) before reversing, which resolves the ordering problem entirely.

For REFUNDED-status invoices, isCommissionableInvoice already returns false, so no accrual ever happens — correct. For wallet-credit refunds where the invoice stays PAID, accruing first then reversing nets out correctly, and the later sweep will just skip since a commission record now exists. Now I'm checking how the sweep's relation filter behaves when excluding invoices that already have a partnerCommission.

I'm also verifying accrueCommissionForInvoice's idempotency still holds under the compound unique constraint on invoiceId and reversalKey — duplicate original accruals still collide and get swallowed as before. Then I'm considering a trickier case: a partial refund happening before accrual, where the invoice is still PAID with a nonzero refundedCents, meaning the initial accrual would compute commission on the full amount rather than accounting for the refund already applied.

I'm weighing whether the sweep needs a reconciliation pass that checks invoices with nonzero refundedCents and ensures a corresponding reversal exists, but that risks conflicting with the event-based idempotency keys already in use, so I'm leaning toward simplifying the refundPayment key scheme instead.

I realize it's cleaner to treat admin-refund reversals as cumulative against invoice.refundedCents specifically, while keeping all other refund sources event-keyed with unique per-step keys since refundedCents only increases via CAS. So refundPayment events use a key like `refund:${total}` with amount equal to the step's cents, and the sweep backstop reconciles admin refunds against that cumulative total.

But the VOID path for accrued commissions doesn't carry a key, which breaks that per-event audit trail — so I'm reconsidering whether to just always use negative rows uniformly instead of a separate VOID status, since a negative ACCRUED row already satisfies the owner's rule for both not-yet-paid and already-paid cases.

Actually, VOIDing the original reads better in the partner ledger than two offsetting rows, and it keeps analytics clean since a voided commission won't be double-counted as a conversion. I'll keep VOID for the simple full-refund case, skip building a sweep backstop for the admin path, and instead make the synchronous reversal hook itself robust by logging an audit event if it fails after commit.

Weighing the realistic failure modes — DB outage or a bug caught in staging — a post-commit best-effort call with audit logging on failure seems adequate, though it's worth considering whether doing the reversal inside the same transaction would be safer and avoid needing a sweep at all, if the unique-constraint conflict issue can be worked around.

Checking each case (refund, cancel, reconcile, domain transfer), the existing CAS guards already ensure each step only proceeds once, so a unique-key collision inside the transaction could really only come from a genuine bug — and letting that roll back the whole transaction is actually the safer, fail-closed behavior since the operation can just be retried.

But I realize the outside-transaction approach has its own failure mode: any unexpected error in the reversal logic could block refunds entirely, which is bad since refunds are money-critical. There's also a subtlety with accrual — running it inside the same transaction risks a P2002 collision with a concurrent sweep, which would abort the refund. It's probably cleaner to do accrual outside the transaction (best-effort) and only the reversal inside it, staying consistent with the codebase's convention of never throwing for no-op cases.

I'll wrap the post-commit call in a safe wrapper that logs failures and records an AuditLog, plus add a lightweight backstop in the sweep for invoice-visible cases. Thinking through the key scheme, I want to treat invoice-ledger refunds as one reversal source, where the cumulative truth is derived from the invoice's REFUNDED status and refundedCents value.

Reversal rows get keyed by that cumulative amount, so a shortfall calculation against already-reversed amounts stays idempotent — the sweep backstop can call the same computation and self-heal since it'll always converge to the same key and result. I'm now working out the second reversal source, off-invoice wallet-credit refunds like prorated cancellations and failed-job refunds, which need their own event-based keys tied to server or job IDs.

I also need to handle the VOID case: if the original charge was still ACCRUED with no prior reversals and this reversal covers the full amount, I should void the record outright rather than writing a reversal row, since a VOID effectively means the whole amount counts as reversed already. To avoid double-counting across sources, I'm defining the delta as the minimum of the per-source shortfall and the overall remaining amount, so that once something's voided, the remaining is zero and everything downstream becomes a no-op.

Thinking about whether this is over-engineered given the actual use case — infrequent refunds mainly through the 72h guarantee via admin refund or dashboard cancel — I want to simplify the implementation while keeping it correct, settling on a single function `reversePartnerCommissionForRefund({ invoiceId, refundCents, key, reason? })` to handle all refund paths.

I'm working through the steps: load the invoice, best-effort accrue commission if still PAID (so full refunds that already flipped status to REFUNDED correctly skip accrual and have nothing to reverse), find the original commission row and check for idempotency against this refund's key, then determine how much has already been reversed based on whether the row was voided.

From there I calculate the remaining reversible amount, derive the refund fraction against the invoice total to figure out the delta to reverse, and if that delta fully consumes an ACCRUED row I try to void it via a compare-and-swap update — falling back to creating a separate REFUND row if the CAS fails because the row got paid out in the meantime.

For `refundPayment`, I key on the new total after refund, and I'm weighing whether a backstop sweep could work using a key derived from the invoice's accumulated refunded amount, though without tagging the source of each step it's hard to know for certain which admin actions have already synced.

3	/**
4	 * Real, historical lifetime revenue for a specific server — including
5	 * add-ons, upgrades and renewals, net of refunds. NOT an estimate (never
6	 * current-plan-price × months-elapsed): every cent comes from actual billing
7	 * records this app already writes.
8	 *
9	 * There is no direct FK from Invoice/WalletTransaction to Server — every
10	 * charge site (lib/order.ts, lib/game-order.ts, worker/billing.ts, lib/resize.ts,
11	 * lib/dedicated-ip-purchase.ts, lib/disk-expand.ts, lib/backup-upgrade.ts,
12	 * lib/game-resize.ts, lib/actions-server-lifecycle.ts) instead embeds the
13	 * server's `hostname` in the Invoice/WalletTransaction `description` string —
14	 * the exact same convention `lib/actions-billing.ts`'s `regenerateMissingInvoices`
15	 * already relies on. This module follows that same convention, scoped
16	 * additionally by `userId` (a server's hostname is unique to begin with, but
17	 * scoping by owner removes any residual cross-customer collision risk
18	 * entirely).
19	 *
20	 * Primary source: Invoice, because it is the actual billing document (what the
21	 * customer sees on /dashboard/invoices, tax-inclusive) and — verified against
22	 * production data — has hostname coverage for every charge type: the initial
23	 * order (VPS AND game), renewals, upgrades, and every add-on (dedicated IP,
24	 * disk, backups). PAID invoices net their own `refundedCents` (an admin
25	 * partial/full refund via `refundPayment` updates the SAME invoice, never
26	 * creates a new one); a small number of cancellations issue a separate
27	 * "credit note" invoice with `status: "REFUNDED"` and a positive `amountCents`
28	 * (see `actions-server-lifecycle.ts`'s immediate-cancel refund) — those are
29	 * subtracted.
30	 *
31	 * Known, verified gap this module corrects for: a mid-term DOWNGRADE credit
32	 * (`actions-server-lifecycle.ts`, "Downgrade to … (prorated credit)") and a
33	 * job-failure refund (worker/index.ts, "Refund: failed …") both only touch
34	 * WalletTransaction — no Invoice is written or adjusted for either. Both are
35	 * folded in as corrections below so they are not silently missed. (A downgrade
36	 * credit that is later clawed back on a failed resize — "Reversed downgrade
37	 * credit …" — is included too, so the two net to zero exactly as they do in
38	 * the customer's real wallet balance.)
39	 *
40	 * Separately verified: the very first WalletTransaction line for a GAME
41	 * server order (lib/game-order.ts, `Game server: <plan> (<family>) — <term>`)
42	 * omits the hostname — unlike every sibling call site. It doesn't normally
43	 * matter here (Invoice is primary and DOES carry the hostname for that same
44	 * charge, since commit 5ecc6eedf4 "Create an Invoice + invoice-new email for
45	 * game-server orders", 2026-08-27) — but any game server ordered BEFORE that
46	 * commit has NO invoice at all, only that hostname-less WalletTransaction
47	 * debit, and would otherwise show $0 lifetime spend despite having genuinely
48	 * paid. Verified against production: exactly this happened to one live
49	 * customer server (terraria-i2ydef, ordered 2026-08-26). Recovered below via
50	 * a time-proximity fallback (same owner, a "Game server:" debit within 60s of
51	 * the server's own `createdAt` — the two rows are written in the same
52	 * transaction, so in practice they land within a couple of milliseconds of
53	 * each other) ONLY when no invoice at all matched this server's hostname, so
54	 * a normal (post-fix) order is never double-counted.
55	 *
56	 * RENAME SAFETY (found live 2026-09-25): a hostname rename — currently only
57	 * `scripts/dedupe-hostnames.ts` — leaves every already-written record holding
58	 * the OLD hostname, which a match keyed off the CURRENT hostname alone would
59	 * never find again (a real dedupe run on 2026-09-24 renamed 6 duplicate
60	 * "web-01" servers and silently zeroed their lifetime spend). Every match
61	 * below therefore checks `Server.previousHostnames` (appended to by the same
62	 * rename that changes `hostname`) alongside the current hostname, so a rename
63	 * can never sever a record from the server that earned it.
64	 */
65	export async function resolveServerLifetimeSpendCents(
66	  servers: { id: string; hostname: string; previousHostnames: string[]; userId: string; createdAt: Date }[],
67	): Promise<Map<string, number>> {
68	  const result = new Map<string, number>();
69	  if (servers.length === 0) return result;
70	
71	  const userIds = Array.from(new Set(servers.map((s) => s.userId)));
72	
73	  const [invoices, corrections, preInvoiceGameOrders] = await Promise.all([
74	    db.invoice.findMany({
75	      where: { userId: { in: userIds }, status: { in: ["PAID", "REFUNDED"] } },
76	      select: { userId: true, description: true, amountCents: true, refundedCents: true, status: true },
77	    }),
78	    db.walletTransaction.findMany({
79	      where: {
80	        userId: { in: userIds },
81	        OR: [
82	          { description: { startsWith: "Downgrade to" } },
83	          { description: { startsWith: "Refund: failed" } },
84	          { description: { startsWith: "Reversed downgrade credit" } },
85	        ],
86	      },
87	      select: { userId: true, description: true, amountCents: true },
88	    }),
89	    // Fallback pool for the pre-5ecc6eedf4 (2026-08-27) gap documented above:
90	    // game-order debits that never got an invoice and don't carry a hostname.
91	    db.walletTransaction.findMany({
92	      where: { userId: { in: userIds }, description: { startsWith: "Game server:" }, amountCents: { lt: 0 } },
93	      select: { userId: true, amountCents: true, createdAt: true },
94	    }),
95	  ]);
96	
97	  // True when `description` embeds the CURRENT hostname or any hostname this
98	  // server was renamed FROM — see the RENAME SAFETY doc above.
99	  const matchesServer = (description: string, s: { hostname: string; previousHostnames: string[] }) =>
100	    description.includes(s.hostname) || s.previousHostnames.some((h) => description.includes(h));
101	
102	  for (const s of servers) {
103	    let cents = 0;
104	    let anyInvoiceMatched = false;
105	
106	    for (const inv of invoices) {
107	      if (inv.userId !== s.userId || !matchesServer(inv.description, s)) continue;
108	      anyInvoiceMatched = true;
109	      if (inv.status === "PAID") {
110	        cents += inv.amountCents - (inv.refundedCents ?? 0);
111	      } else if (inv.status === "REFUNDED") {
112	        // A standalone credit-note invoice (e.g. "Cancellation refund — host")
113	        // — its amountCents is the positive amount returned to the customer.
114	        cents -= inv.amountCents;
115	      }
116	    }
117	
118	    for (const c of corrections) {
119	      if (c.userId !== s.userId || !matchesServer(c.description, s)) continue;
120	      // amountCents > 0 (Downgrade credit, failed-job refund) reduces spend;
121	      // amountCents < 0 (a clawed-back downgrade credit) restores it.
122	      cents -= c.amountCents;
123	    }
124	
125	    if (!anyInvoiceMatched) {
126	      const fallback = preInvoiceGameOrders.find(
127	        (t) => t.userId === s.userId && Math.abs(t.createdAt.getTime() - s.createdAt.getTime()) <= 60_000,
128	      );
129	      if (fallback) cents += -fallback.amountCents;
130	    }
131	
132	    result.set(s.id, Math.max(0, cents));
133	  }
134	
135	  return result;
136	}

#!/bin/bash
# Deploy a ref (default: main from /opt/nxeon) to the staging environment.
# Usage: ./scripts/deploy-staging.sh [git-ref]
set -euo pipefail
REF="${1:-main}"
cd /opt/nxeon-staging

echo "==> Syncing staging to $REF"
git fetch origin
git reset --hard "origin/$REF"

echo "==> Installing dependencies"
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -1

echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss 2>&1 | tail -2
npm run db:seed 2>&1 | tail -2 || true

echo "==> Building"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4

# next.config sets output:"standalone" but the systemd unit runs the standalone
# server.js directly (not `next start`, which Next.js explicitly does not
# support alongside output:"standalone" — it prints a warning and silently
# fails to resolve some routes, confirmed live 2026-09-10: a brand-new API
# route 404'd under `next start` on this exact build and returned 200 under
# `node .next/standalone/server.js`). The standalone output does NOT include
# public/ or .next/static/ (Next's own documented behavior) — copy them in
# fresh every build, or every static asset/route added after the last copy
# is missing until the next deploy happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static
cp -r public .next/standalone/public
cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
# geoip-lite is in next.config.ts's serverExternalPackages (kept OUT of the JS
# bundle on purpose, since it reads .dat files off its own package path at
# runtime) — but the standalone output tracer only copies files it can trace
# as JS-imported, so an externalized package's own non-JS data files are
# silently left behind. Found live 2026-09-10: this crashed EVERY request
# with an uncaught ENOENT the moment the systemd unit ran the standalone
# server.js instead of `next start` — geo-ip.ts's own try/catch around
# geoip.lookup() does NOT help, because the failure isn't confined to that
# call. Copy the package's real data/ directory in every build, same
# reasoning as public/.next/static above.
if [ -d node_modules/geoip-lite/data ]; then
  mkdir -p .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data
  cp -r node_modules/geoip-lite/data/. .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data/
fi

# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. Only .next needs to be writable by
# it (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable, and systemd
# injects .env as root. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon-staging/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon-staging/.env 2>/dev/null || true

echo "==> Restarting staging services"
systemctl restart nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-staging-web nxeon-staging-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1:8080/)
echo "==> Staging responds: HTTP $CODE (http://$(grep ^PUBLIC_IP .env | cut -d= -f2):8080)"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "STAGING UNHEALTHY"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Staging deploy complete"

37:# Postgres server, confirmed live) — deploy-staging.sh's own `db push` only
43:# failure gave any warning, since staging's own db push had already
44:# succeeded there). `db push` both applies the schema AND regenerates the

content.thinking:
The prisma validate output was just a version notice, so generation succeeded. Now I'm writing the commission reversal logic in lib/partner-commission.ts, defining a function that reverses a partner's commission when a refund occurs, keyed by invoice ID and refund amount.

I'm laying out the validation steps: guard against invalid invoice IDs, non-positive refund amounts, or missing keys; fetch the invoice and its commissionable fields; if the invoice is still PAID, trigger accrual to ensure the original commission exists before reversing; then look up existing commission rows to find the original entry.

Next, I calculate how much has already been reversed—accounting for either a VOID status or the sum of prior REFUND rows—then figure the remaining reversible amount. I compute the proportional refund share based on the ratio of refundCents to the invoice total, capping it at the original commission amount, and take the smaller of that desired amount versus what's actually still remaining to reverse.

For an ACCRUED commission being fully reversed with nothing yet applied, I attempt a direct status update to VOID with a concurrency check—if another process already settled it to PAID, I fall back to creating a REFUND row instead. I'm also considering idempotency: a repeat call with the same key against an already-VOID commission should safely resolve to no remaining amount and return null.

I'll log each reversal in the audit log with the action type, invoice, partner, and dollar amount, keeping the userId nullable for system-initiated actions. For partial reversals, I create a REFUND-kind commission row with negative amounts proportional to the original base and rate, using the reversal key to prevent duplicate inserts via a unique constraint violation.

I realize concurrent reversals on the same invoice could race and over-reverse the commission if they each compute remaining amounts from the same snapshot. To fix this properly, I should wrap the reversal logic in a transaction that locks the original commission row with a raw SELECT FOR UPDATE query, forcing concurrent reversals to serialize on that lock rather than relying solely on the unique key constraint.

I also need to consider how this interacts with settlement logic — if an admin concurrently settles the commission from ACCRUED to PAID, the row lock ensures that transaction blocks until ours commits, then its conditional update re-evaluates against the new status, correctly preventing a settlement of a commission that's just been voided.

For the wrapper function, I'm designing it to never throw for callers in money-critical paths: catching errors, logging them, and writing an audit log entry, while making the core exported function itself throw on genuine DB failures per the spec requiring real errors to propagate.

I'm also writing a helper that computes the cumulative refunded amount recorded directly on an invoice, using the invoice's status and refund fields to determine the true refunded total, then sketching a sync function that reconciles partner commission against that invoice-level refund figure.

I'm checking edge cases: when a full refund voids the original commission without leaving a "ledger:" tracking row, the next sync run should just compute a no-op reversal safely; when refunds are partial, each new ledger entry should track how much has already been covered so subsequent syncs only reverse the incremental difference.

But I'm worried about races outside the locking mechanism — if two syncs for overlapping refund amounts read the "covered" value before the other's write commits, they could both compute overlapping reversal targets using a stale covered amount, since admin refund commits are serialized by compare-and-swap but the post-commit reversal calls themselves may run concurrently.

The fix is to compute the covered amount inside the lock, so I want to restructure the reversal core to accept a function that computes the refund amount from the locked rows rather than a fixed value. For event-based reversals this function just returns the fixed refundCents, while for ledger-based ones it recomputes covered minus the total from the locked rows, with the key still derived from the pre-lock invoice read.

I also need to grab the original record's id before the transaction, then lock and re-read all rows inside it. For accrual-first logic, I'm checking what invoice fields `accrueCommissionForInvoice` needs, and considering edge cases like prorated refunds on renewal invoices that never accrued because the customer attached after the invoice was created — the existing accrual guards should handle that correctly.

I'm also confirming that accruing commission on a PAUSED partner just returns null safely, and that reversals still route to the original partner even if the customer later detaches. For the summary calculations, I want to add a signed `balanceCents` (lifetime minus paid) so the UI can show a "carried debit" note when it goes negative, and I need to update the admin settle-commission error message to handle the case where there's nothing to settle due to a negative balance.

I'm also tracing through settlement logic: when outstanding is positive, all ACCRUED rows (including negative REFUND rows) flip to PAID correctly. But if outstanding is zero or negative while ACCRUED rows still exist, nothing settles yet — those rows stay pending until a future month's accrual pushes the balance positive again, at which point everything settles together. And for recording a payout, I'm confirming it rejects amounts exceeding outstanding, with negative balances treated as zero outstanding.

Now I'm looking at how analytics and dashboards handle REFUND rows: the commission sums correctly net out negatives, and the status sums by group also net correctly. But the "charges" count is currently counting REFUND rows as if they were charges, which is a minor inaccuracy I should fix by excluding REFUND kind from that count.

For the partner per-customer view, the charge count similarly includes REFUND rows, which would mislead a partner into thinking they had more charges than actual — I'll add a second small groupBy with a kind filter to compute the accurate charge count separately, since fixing it in the main aggregation would incorrectly exclude refund reversals from earned totals.

Now I'm checking other spots affected by VOID becoming a real status: the per-customer aggregate summing amountCents across all statuses would now wrongly include VOID rows in lifetime totals, so I need to add a status exclusion there too, since that's a direct consequence of my change making VOID rows actually occur. The admin partners list grandOutstanding/grandPaid sums look fine since they filter by specific statuses. But the partnerFunnel conversion count groups by customerId across all statuses including VOID, meaning a fully refunded customer would still count as "converted" — I should add the same VOID exclusion there for consistency with how analytics defines conversions.

I'm deciding to exclude VOID rows from the funnel conversion query too, since a customer who got fully refunded within the window arguably shouldn't count as converted, and this keeps the definition consistent with the analytics conversion logic. Next I want to check how the UI renders commission rows by kind/status, so I'm going to look at the partner dashboard component and the admin detail table to confirm REFUND rows and negative amounts display sensibly.

content.content:
**Data model** (`prisma/schema.prisma`):

| Model | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ReferralPartner` | The partner: `code` (unique, uppercase), `commissionRatePct` (per-partner, frozen onto each commission row at accrual), `status` (ACTIVE/PAUSED — pausing stops BOTH new commission AND the customer discount), optional `userId` login |
| `PartnerCustomer` | The lifetime attachment. `customerId` UNIQUE — one partner per customer, ever. `firstPurchaseDiscountUsedAt` (null until their first discounted purchase; null = 50% tier, set = 10% tier forever) |
| `PartnerCommission` | One row per qualifying PAID invoice, `invoiceId` UNIQUE (idempotent). `baseCents` = net charge minus that invoice's `dedicatedIpCents` — the dedicated-IP exclusion |
| `PartnerPayout` | A REAL payment made to the partner off-wallet (bank/Wise/PayPal), can be partial. Balance = `sum(PartnerCommission, status != VOID) − sum(PartnerPayout)` — NOT derived from commission-row status alone (see the model's own doc comment for why a partial payout needs a separate ledger) |
| `PartnerInvite` | Two kinds (`kind`). `LOGIN`: a pending invite for a brand-new (non-customer) login on an admin-made partner — token-hash/expiry, mirrors `OrgInvite`'s mechanics. `CREATOR` (2026-09-27): an invite made BEFORE any partner exists — `partnerId` is null until claimed; carries `name`, `note`, `ratePct`, `allowAnyEmail`, the CSV prefill (`channelUrl`, `primaryGame`, `country`, `subscribers`), `lastSentAt` (NULL = DRAFT, never emailed) and `sendCount` |
| `PartnerPayoutProfile` (2026-09-27) | One per partner: the partner's own contact fields (plain) + preferred payout method; the method-specific details and note are sealed in `payoutDetailsEnc` with `lib/crypto-box.ts` (AES-256-GCM from `AUTH_SECRET`). `payoutUpdatedAt` shown to admins |
| `ReferralClick` (existing, previously unused) | One row per real link click — `code`, `ipHash`, `referer`, `convertedUserId` (best-effort, set at registration to the most recent unconverted click for that code) |
| `Invoice.dedicatedIpCents` | How much of that invoice's net amount is the dedicated-IP surcharge — a real typed column, populated by every charge path that can bill one (`lib/order.ts`, `lib/game-order.ts`, `worker/billing.ts`), never inferred by parsing line items after the fact |

**The links.** `nxeon.cloud/partner/<code>` (`app/partner/[code]/route.ts`) is the REAL link partners
are given — it records a `ReferralClick` row, then sets the `nxeon_ref` cookie and 302s to
....
- **Domains** never carry this discount (spec). Coupons remain VPS/game only (`CouponServiceKind`
  has no hosting/email value); a code typed on a hosting/email order is answered "Promo codes apply
  to Cloud VPS and Game Server orders only." instead of being silently ignored.

**Commission dedicated-IP exclusion** — `commissionableBaseCents(netCents, dedicatedIpCents)`
(`lib/partner-commission.ts`, pure, unit-tested) = `max(0, netCents − dedicatedIpCents)`. Every
accrual path (`accrueCommissionForInvoice`, called by the inline post-order/post-renewal hooks AND
the background `reconcilePartnerCommissions` sweep) reads `Invoice.dedicatedIpCents` and excludes it
— never a string match against a line-item description.

**Admin** (`/admin/partners`, `/admin/partners/[id]`, `lib/actions-partner.ts`,
`components/admin/PartnerControls.tsx`): create/manage partners and rates (existing), attach/detach
customers (existing), plus new: real click→signup→conversion funnel (`partnerFunnel`), the real
`/partner/<code>` link, **invite a brand-new login** (`adminCreatePartnerInvite` — a public accept
page at `/partner/invite/accept?token=...` creates the account, since the invitee has none yet;
mirrors `OrgInvite`'s token/hash/expiry, not its `requireUser()`-gated redemption), and **record a
partial/specific payout** (`adminRecordPartnerPayout`) alongside the existing full-settle
(`adminSettlePartnerCommission`, now payout-ledger-aware).

**Partner portal — tabs (2026-09-27).** `/dashboard/partner` is split into seven tabs driven by
`?tab=` (linkable, survives refresh; resolved server-side in `app/dashboard/partner/page.tsx`, then
the client switches tabs with the native History API so no server round trip is needed; a
WAI-ARIA tablist with roving focus — ←/→/Home/End). Tab list: `lib/nx/partner-tabs.ts`.
- **Overview** — lifetime stat tiles, all-time click/signup/conversion funnel, the partner link +
  share buttons + code, "What you earn", and a nudge to add a payout method if none is saved.
- **Analytics** — `lib/partner-analytics.ts`, computed server-side for `?range=7d|30d|90d|12m|all`
  or `range=custom&from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD` (UTC days; ≤45 days bucket by day, ≤200 by week,
  else month; an unreadable custom range falls back to 30 days and says so). Real sources only:
  clicks = `ReferralClick` for the code; signups = `PartnerCustomer.attachedAt`; paying conversions
  = a customer's FIRST non-void `PartnerCommission`; commission = `PartnerCommission` (pending =
  ACCRUED, settled = PAID, VOID excluded); "paid to you" = `PartnerPayout`. Rates are cohort-honest:
  "led to a signup" = clicks with `convertedUserId` ÷ clicks; "have paid" = of this range's signups,
  how many have ever paid. Charts are three small-multiple bar charts (one y-axis each) + a
  commission bar chart — `components/ui/bar-chart.tsx`, dependency-free SVG, measures its own width,
  hover/keyboard tooltip, "View as table". **Top sources** = the `ReferralClick.referer` host
  (many apps send no referrer → "Direct / not shared"; there is no UTM capture). The events table

assert s.count(anchor)==1
entry='''## Refunds and chargebacks now reverse partner commission (2026-09-29)

**The gap:** a refunded or charged-back charge kept its partner commission. No refund path
(`lib/actions-admin-billing.ts`, `lib/actions-server-lifecycle.ts`, `lib/domain-transfer.ts`, the
worker's failed-job refunds) touched `PartnerCommission`, so a partner stayed owed — or kept, if
already paid — commission on money that went back to the customer. Worse with wallet-credit refunds:
the customer re-spends the credit, that new invoice earns commission again, and the partner is paid
twice for one real payment.

**The owner's rule** (verbatim in the Creator Partner Program section above): a refund/chargeback
comes off the commission; unpaid → off what's owed now, already paid out → off the next payout;
the partner is never billed back.

**Schema** (`prisma/schema.prisma`, applied with the usual `prisma db push`):
`PartnerCommission.invoiceId @unique` → new column `reversalKey String @default("")` +
`@@unique([invoiceId, reversalKey])`; `kind` gains `"REFUND"`; `Invoice.partnerCommission?` →
`Invoice.partnerCommissions[]`. The DDL `db push` runs (checked with `prisma migrate diff` against
both staging and production — read-only on prod): `DROP INDEX "PartnerCommission_invoiceId_key"`,
`ADD COLUMN "reversalKey" TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX
"PartnerCommission_invoiceId_reversalKey_key"`. Every existing row gets `''`, and existing invoiceIds
are already unique, so the new index can't collide. Chosen over `@@unique([invoiceId, kind])`
because (a) every original row shares the SAME empty key, so "one original per invoice" is exactly
as strong as the old bare unique regardless of which of ORDER/RENEWAL/CHARGE the description
infers, and (b) two partial refunds on one invoice — an ordinary support sequence, see
`refundPayment`'s own comments — each need their own reversal row; a per-kind unique allows only one.

**Engine, wiring, chargebacks, display:** see "Refunds and chargebacks reverse commission" in the
Creator Partner Program section above.

**Files:** `prisma/schema.prisma`, `lib/partner-commission.ts`, `lib/actions-admin-billing.ts`,
`lib/actions-server-lifecycle.ts`, `lib/server-spend.ts`, `lib/domain-transfer.ts`,
`lib/disk-expand.ts`, `lib/dedicated-ip-purchase.ts`, `lib/resize.ts`, `worker/index.ts`,
`lib/actions-partner.ts`, `components/admin/PartnerControls.tsx`, `app/admin/invoices/[id]/page.tsx`,
`app/admin/partners/[id]/page.tsx`, `app/dashboard/partner/page.tsx`, `components/nx/PartnerView.tsx`,
`lib/partner-analytics.ts`, `test/partner-commission-reversal.test.ts`, `ROADMAP.md`.

'''
s=s.replace(anchor, entry+anchor,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

**Verified on staging (2026-09-29), real DB, real admin UI.** Deployed as a staging-only merge

kept its `ServerMemSample` table). `db push` applied exactly the three statements above; the 11
pre-existing staging commission rows all got `reversalKey ''`, nothing else changed. A dedicated
test partner (`RFNDE54F4A`, 40%) + customer with real PAID invoices, accrued by the real
`accrueRecentCommissionsForCustomer` — $32.80 owed across 6 charges — then (balance = earned − paid):
- **Unpaid, full refund** — admin UI "Refund" $10.00 on invoice #73: commission $4.00 ACCRUED → VOID;
  owed $32.80 → $28.80. UI message reports the reversal.
- **Unpaid, two partial refunds** — $5.00 then $3.00 on the $13.99 invoice #75: REFUND rows −$2.00
  (`ledger:500`) and −$1.20 (`ledger:800`) = exactly round(5.60 × 8.00/13.99); owed → $25.60.
- **Cancellation-style** ($9.70 of a $10.00 term, `latestServerTermInvoiceId` picked the term
  invoice, not the later add-on) → −$3.88; same key again → no-op. **Failed-job-style** full refund
  of a $3.00 add-on → its $1.20 VOIDed. Owed → $20.52.
- **Settlement** — admin UI "Mark $20.52 paid": one $20.52 payout, every ACCRUED row incl. the

- **Already paid, full refund** — UI refund $20.00 on invoice #74: original stays PAID, new REFUND

  "-$18.00 carried", no payout possible, nothing collected.

input.title: Exclude standalone dedicated-IP purchases from commission
input.tldr: While fixing refund reversal of partner commission, I found the standalone "add a dedicated IP" purchase creates its invoice without the dedicated-IP amount recorded, so partners earn full commission on it despite the 0% dedicated-IP rule. The new session will record it and add a test.
input.prompt:
Nxeon (repo /opt/nxeon, Next.js + Prisma; read CLAUDE.md first — work in a fresh git worktree off main, never run `npm run build` in /opt/nxeon, deploy via scripts/deploy-staging.sh, do not promote to production without owner sign-off).

Bug: the Creator Partner Program's rule is that a partner earns 0% commission on the dedicated-IP add-on (see docs/DOCUMENTATION.md "Creator Partner Program" section and `commissionableBaseCents` in lib/partner-commission.ts, which subtracts `Invoice.dedicatedIpCents` from the commission base). Every charge path that can bill a dedicated IP is supposed to populate `Invoice.dedicatedIpCents` (schema comment on the Invoice model lists lib/order.ts, lib/game-order.ts, worker/billing.ts commitRenewal). Fix: pass `dedicatedIpCents: prorateCents` in that invoiceCreateData call (the whole invoice is the dedicated IP). Check whether any other add-on path bills a dedicated IP without setting it (grep invoiceCreateData callers). Add a unit/source test in the style of test/partner-discount.test.ts. Read-only check prod (`sudo -u postgres psql -d nxeon`) for existing PartnerCommission rows on invoices whose description starts with "Dedicated IP add-on" and report them to the owner (do not alter prod data). input.title: Refund failed game-server tier changes
input.tldr: While wiring commission reversal into the worker's failed-job refunds, I noticed a game-server tier change that fails never refunds its prorated charge, because its job carries no charge amount. The new session will make it refund like VPS upgrades do.
input.prompt:
Nxeon (repo /opt/nxeon, Next.js + Prisma; read CLAUDE.md first — work in a fresh git worktree off main, never run `npm run build` in /opt/nxeon, deploy via scripts/deploy-staging.sh, do not promote to production without owner sign-off).

Bug: `applyGameResize` in lib/game-resize.ts debits the wallet and writes a PAID invoice ("Tier change to <plan> (prorated) — <hostname>") for `quote.prorateCents`, then enqueues a RESIZE job with payload `{ planId, gamePlanId }` only. The worker's terminal-failure reconciliation, `reconcileFailedJob` in worker/index.ts, reverses a RESIZE's money only when `payload.prorateCents > 0` (and uses `payload.direction`), so a failed GAME tier change never refunds the customer. Compare lib/resize.ts `applyResize`, which records `{ planId, prorateCents, direction: "up", invoiceId }` on its job payload.

Fix: record `prorateCents`, `direction: "up"` (only when prorateCents > 0 — check whether a game tier DOWN-grade exists and how it's credited, so a down-reversal isn't mis-handled) and the created invoice's id as `invoiceId` on the game RESIZE job payload, so the existing reconcile path refunds it — and, via the invoiceId, also reverses any partner commission on that charge (see `reverseCommissionForFailedJob` in worker/index.ts, added on branch fix/refund-commission-reversal; if that branch isn't merged yet, coordinate or rebase onto it). Verify on staging. Update docs/DOCUMENTATION.md (dated changelog entry) and ROADMAP.md per the repo's house rule.

input.message:
## Summary

Refunds and chargebacks now reverse partner commission, following the owner's rule. The branch is **`fix/refund-commission-reversal`** (commits c567580a68 and a3953d6fd4), pushed to GitHub. It is **not merged into main and not promoted.** It changes the schema and touches partner money, so the owner should review it first.

- **Worktree:** /root/nxeon-worktrees/refund-commission, branched off origin/main 714fe37706 (local main in /opt/nxeon was 3 commits behind).
- **node_modules:** a private copy of the Prisma client, so /opt/nxeon's generated client was never touched (checksum confirmed).
- **Checks:** `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean. The full test suite has the same 40 failures as the baseline commit and no new ones; the 5 new tests pass.

## Every real refund path found (grep across lib/, worker/, app/api)

1. **Admin `refundPayment`** (lib/actions-admin-billing.ts). This is the admin path for the 72-hour guarantee and any partial or full admin refund. It is tied to an invoice and tracks `refundedCents`. **Wired.**
2. **Self-serve `cancelService` immediate termination** (lib/actions-server-lifecycle.ts). This is the dashboard path for the guarantee: a prorated wallet refund. **Wired.** The invoice it reverses is found by the new `latestServerTermInvoiceId` in lib/server-spend.ts, which reuses the "(hostname)" / previousHostnames matching the codebase already uses.
3. **`settleFailedTransferIn`** (lib/domain-transfer.ts). This covers both the worker path and the customer's cancel-transfer path, and flips the invoice to REFUNDED. **Wired.**
4. **Worker failed-job refunds** in worker/index.ts: disk expansion, dedicated-IP purchase and VPS upgrade. **Wired.** The charge sites (lib/disk-expand.ts, lib/dedicated-ip-purchase.ts, lib/resize.ts) now put `invoiceId` on the job payload. Jobs queued before deploy don't carry it and are skipped.
5. **Deliberately not reversed:**
   - A failed domain registration refund: domain registrations create no invoice, so they never earn commission.
   - A mid-term downgrade credit: it's a plan change, not a refund. The owner may want to decide on this one.
   - Admin balance adjustments.
6. **Chargebacks: no code path existed at all.** There is no Stripe dispute webhook, and wallet-funded invoices can't be traced back to one card charge. I added an admin **"Record chargeback"** button to a new "Partner commission" card on /admin/invoices/[id]. It is `adminReverseCommissionForChargeback`: billing area only, one per invoice, and it changes the partner ledger only, nothing on the customer side.

## Exact schema change

On `PartnerCommission`:
- `invoiceId @unique` is replaced by a new column `reversalKey String @default("")` plus `@@unique([invoiceId, reversalKey])`.
- `kind` gains `"REFUND"`.
- `Invoice.partnerCommission?` becomes `partnerCommissions[]`, and the two relation filters that used it were updated.

`prisma migrate diff` (read-only against prod) shows the DDL is exactly three statements:
- `DROP INDEX "PartnerCommission_invoiceId_key"`
- `ADD COLUMN "reversalKey" TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`
- `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX (invoiceId, reversalKey)`

I used this instead of the suggested `@@unique([invoiceId, kind])` for two reasons:
- Every original row has the same empty key, so "one original per invoice" stays exactly as strong as before, whichever kind the description infers.
- Two partial refunds on one invoice (which `refundPayment`'s own comments call an ordinary support sequence) each need their own reversal row. A per-kind unique allows only one.

## How it works

The engine is in lib/partner-commission.ts:
- **`reversePartnerCommissionForRefund({invoiceId, refundCents, key})`** handles one refund event.
- **`syncPartnerCommissionWithInvoiceRefunds(invoiceId)`** reverses whatever the invoice's own record shows was refunded, using the key `ledger:<cumulative refunded cents>`.

The rules:
- **Unpaid, full refund:** the original row is set to VOID.
- **Already paid, or a partial refund:** a negative REFUND row is written as ACCRUED, so it nets into the next settlement.
- **Amounts:** reversals are proportional to the share refunded and capped at what's left of the commission.

Safety measures:
- It accrues the original commission first if the sweep hadn't reached that charge yet.
- It runs under a row lock on the original commission, so concurrent refunds can't over-reverse.
- Hooks run after the refund commits, through a wrapper that never throws and writes an audit row on failure.
- The worker sweep now also reverses any refund recorded on an invoice whose hook didn't run.

Settlement and payouts:
- `computePartnerSummary` now returns a signed `balanceCents`.
- Settle and record-payout refuse to pay while the balance is at or below zero, so a negative payout can't happen.
- The admin partner page and the partner's Payouts tab both show the carried negative balance.

## Verified on staging with real numbers (real admin UI + real DB)

Test partner RFNDE54F4A at 40%, owed $32.80 after the real accrual function ran:
- **Unpaid, full refund:** UI refund of $10.00 → that $4.00 commission went to VOID. Owed $32.80 → $28.80.
- **Unpaid, two partial refunds:** $5 then $3 on a $13.99 charge → rows of −$2.00 and −$1.20 (exactly 5.60 × 8/13.99). Owed → $25.60.
- **Cancellation-style and failed-job-style reversals:** −$3.88, and a $1.20 commission voided. Retrying with the same key did nothing. Owed → $20.52.
- **Settlement:** UI "Mark paid" recorded a $20.52 payout, and every row, including the negative ones, moved to PAID.
- **Already paid out:**
  - UI refund of $20 → the original stays PAID and a −$8.00 REFUND row is added.
  - UI chargeback of $25 → −$10.00; a second submit was refused.
  - Balance is now −$18.00. Settle is disabled and the page shows "-$18.00 carried".
- **Carry-forward:** $22 of new commission was earned, and the next UI settlement paid **$4.00** (22 − 18).
- **Paid, partial:** a $25 refund on a $50 charge → −$10.00, and the partner's own dashboard shows the carried-deduction note.
- **Sweep backstop:** reversed 1, then 0 on a second pass. **Refund before accrual:** accrued, then voided. **Real `settleFailedTransferIn` call:** $5.20 voided, and the retry did nothing.

Prod, read-only: 12 ACCRUED rows ($21.35), 0 PAID, 0 payouts, and no refunded invoices for any partner customer, so there is nothing historic to back-reverse.

## Things you should know

- **Staging deploy:** staging was carrying `merge-mem-temp`, which includes the memory fix and its `ServerMemSample` table. Deploying my branch alone would have dropped that table and reverted the memory fix on staging. So I deployed `merge-refund-temp` (merge-mem-temp + my branch), a local branch in /opt/nxeon. Staging is healthy at e561b226.
- **Promote hazard, independent of this change:** prod's database already has `ServerMemSample`, but main's schema doesn't. Any promote of main without `fix/accurate-memory-reporting` lets `db push --accept-data-loss` drop that table. Merge this branch together with or after that one.
- **Staging admin hostname:** it is proxied by nginx to node-2 (178.63.94.114:3001), not to /opt/nxeon-staging. So code deployed by deploy-staging.sh isn't visible at that hostname.
- **Stale staging password:** the admin password in /root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt is stale; I did not reset it. I reached this box's staging app directly using a temporary staging-only BILLING test account and a partner-login test account. Both are now suspended with passwords disabled, and the temp credentials file was shredded.
- **Test data left on staging:** the partner RFNDE54F4A and its test customer/invoices are still there for the owner to look at. They are clearly labelled as staging tests.
- **Docs:** docs/DOCUMENTATION.md has an updated Creator Partner Program reference and a dated changelog entry with the numbers above. ROADMAP.md is updated. I did not run publish-docs.
- **Task chips:** I added two for bugs found along the way:
  - Standalone dedicated-IP purchases don't set `dedicatedIpCents`, so partners earn commission on them despite the 0% rule.
  - Failed game-server tier changes are never refunded, because their job payload carries no charge amount.

  I also dismissed the existing chip "Void partner commission when a charge is refunded", since this branch covers it.
